verses.zh: 耶和华晓谕摩西、亚伦说：
verses.en: The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron:

verses.zh: 「人的肉皮上若长了疖子，或长了癣，或长了火斑，在他肉皮上成了大麻疯的灾病，就要将他带到祭司亚伦或亚伦作祭司的一个子孙面前。
verses.en: “When someone has[NOTE:1] a swelling[NOTE:2] or a scab[NOTE:3] or a bright spot[NOTE:4] on the skin of his body[NOTE:5] that may become a diseased infection,[NOTE:6] he must be brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons, the priests.[NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “A man, if [or when] he has….” The term for “a man, human being” (אָדָם, ʾadam; see the note on Lev 1:2) in this case refers to any person among “mankind,” male or female, since either could be afflicted with infections on the skin.

Some of the terms for disease or symptoms of disease in this chapter present difficulties for the translator. Most modern English versions render the Hebrew term שְׂאֵת (seʾet) as “swelling,” which has been retained here (see the explanation in J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 189). Some have argued that “deeper (עָמֹק, ʿamoq) than the skin of his body” in v. 3 means that “this sore was lower than the surrounding skin” (J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:773), in which case “swelling” would be an inappropriate translation of שְׂאֵת in v. 2. Similarly, שְׂאֵת also occurs in v. 19, and then v. 20 raises the issue of whether or not it appears to be “lower (שָׁפָל, shafal) than the skin” (cf. also 14:37 for a mark on the wall of a house), which may mean that the sore sinks below the surface of the skin rather than protruding above it as a swelling would (B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 76-77). Thus, one could translate here, for example, “discoloration” (so Milgrom and II שְׂאֵת “spot, blemish on the skin” in HALOT 1301 s.v. II שְׂאֵת) or “local inflammation, boil, mole” (so Levine). However, one could interpret “lower” as “deeper,” i.e., visibly extending below the surface of the skin into the deeper layers as suggested by J. E. Hartley, Leviticus (WBC), 188, 192. “Swelling” often extends deeply below the surface of the skin, it is certainly a common symptom of skin diseases, and the alternation of these two terms (i.e., “deeper” and “lower”) in vv. 25-26 below shows that they both refer to the same phenomenon (see also the note on v. 20 below), so it is retained in the present translation.
The etymology and meaning of this term is unknown. It could mean “scab” (KJV, ASV, NASB) or possibly “rash” (NIV, NLT), “flaking skin,” or an “eruption” (NRSV) of some sort.
Heb “shiny spot” or “white spot,” but to render this term “white spot” in this chapter would create redundancy in v. 4 where the regular term for “white” occurs alongside this word for “bright spot.”
Heb “in the skin of his flesh” as opposed to the head or the beard (v. 29).

Heb “a mark [or stroke; or plague] of disease.” In some places in this context (vv. 2, 3) it could be translated “a contagious skin disease.” Although the Hebrew term צָרָעַת (tsaraʿat) rendered here “diseased” is translated in many English versions as “leprosy,” it does not refer to Hanson’s disease, which is the modern technical understanding of the term “leprosy” (HALOT 1057 s.v. צָרְעַת a). There has been much discussion of the proper meaning of the term and the disease(s) to which it may refer (see, e.g., J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:774-76, 816-26; J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 187-89; and the literature cited by them). The further description of the actual condition in the text suggests that the regulations are concerned with any kind of infectious diseases that are observable on the surface of the skin and, in addition to that, penetrate below the surface of the skin (vv. 3-4) or spread further across the surface of the skin (vv. 5-8). It is true that, in the OT, the term “disease” is often associated specifically with white “scaly” skin diseases that resemble the wasting away of the skin after death (see Milgrom who, in fact, translates “scale disease”; cf., e.g., Exod 4:6-7 and Num 12:9-12, esp. v. 12), but here it appears to be a broader term for any skin disease that penetrates deep or spreads far on the body. Scaly skin diseases would be included in this category, but also other types. Thus, a “swelling,” “scab,” or “bright spot” on the skin might be a symptom of disease, but not necessarily so. In this sense, “diseased” is a technical term. The term “infection” can apply to any “mark” on the skin whether it belongs to the category of “disease” or not (compare and contrast v. 3, where the “infection” is not “diseased,” with v. 4, where the “infection” is found to be “diseased”).

Or “it shall be reported to Aaron the priest.” This alternative rendering may be better in light of the parallel use of the same expression in Lev 14:2, where the priest had to go outside the camp in order to inspect the person who had been diseased. Since the rendering “he shall be brought to Aaron the priest” might confuse matters there, this expression should be rendered “it shall be reported” both here in 13:2 (cf. also v. 9) and in 14:2. See, however, the further note on 14:2 below, where it is argued that the diseased person would still need to “be brought” to the priest even if this happened outside the camp. Most English versions retain the idea of the afflicted person being “brought” to the priest for inspection.

verses.zh: 祭司要察看肉皮上的灾病，若灾病处的毛已经变白，灾病的现象深于肉上的皮，这便是大麻疯的灾病。祭司要察看他，定他为不洁净。
verses.en: The priest must then examine the infection[NOTE:1] on the skin of the body, and if the hair[NOTE:2] in the infection has turned white and the infection appears to be deeper than the skin of the body,[NOTE:3] then it is a diseased infection,[NOTE:4] so when the priest examines it,[NOTE:5] he must pronounce the person unclean.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see the infection.”
There is no “if” expressed, but the contrast between the priestly finding in this verse and the next verse clearly implies it.
See the note on v. 20 below.
For the translation “diseased infection” see the note on v. 2 above. Cf. TEV “a dreaded skin disease”; NIV11 “a defiling skin disease”; NLT “a contagious skin disease.”
The pronoun “it” here refers to the “infection,” not the person who has the infection (cf. the object of “examine” at the beginning of the verse).

Heb “he shall make him unclean.” The verb is the Piel of טָמֵא (tameʾ) “to be unclean.” Here it is a so-called “declarative” Piel (i.e., “to declare unclean”), but it also implies that the person is put into the category of actually being “unclean” by the pronouncement itself (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 175; cf. the corresponding opposite in v. 6 below).

verses.zh: 若火斑在他肉皮上是白的，现象不深于皮，其上的毛也没有变白，祭司就要将有灾病的人关锁七天。
verses.en: “If[NOTE:1] it is a white bright spot on the skin of his body, but it does not appear to be deeper than the skin,[NOTE:2] and the hair has not turned white, then the priest is to quarantine the person with the infection for seven days.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and if.”
Heb “and deep is not its appearance from the skin”; cf. NAB “does not seem to have penetrated below the skin.”
Heb “and the priest will shut up the infection seven days.”

verses.zh: 第七天，祭司要察看他，若看灾病止住了，没有在皮上发散，祭司还要将他关锁七天。
verses.en: The priest must then examine it on the seventh day, and if,[NOTE:1] as far as he can see, the infection has stayed the same[NOTE:2] and has not spread on the skin,[NOTE:3] then the priest is to quarantine the person for another seven days.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “the infection has stood in his eyes”; ASV “if in his eyes the plague be at a stay.”
Although there is no expressed “and” at the beginning of this clause, there is in the corresponding clause of v. 6, so it should be assumed here as well.
Heb “a second seven days.”

verses.zh: 第七天，祭司要再察看他，若灾病发暗，而且没有在皮上发散，祭司要定他为洁净，原来是癣；那人就要洗衣服，得为洁净。
verses.en: The priest must then examine it again on the seventh day,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the infection has faded and has not spread on the skin, then the priest is to pronounce the person clean.[NOTE:3] It is a scab,[NOTE:4] so he must wash his clothes[NOTE:5] and be clean.
notes: That is, at the end of the second set of seven days referred to at the end of v. 5, a total of fourteen days after the first appearance before the priest.
Heb “and behold.”

Heb “he shall make him clean.” The verb is the Piel of טָהֵר (taher, “to be clean”). Here it is a so-called “declarative” Piel (i.e., “to declare clean”), but it also implies that the person is put into the category of being “clean” by the pronouncement itself (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 176; cf. the corresponding opposite in v. 3 above).
On the term “scab” see the note on v. 2 above. Cf. NAB “it was merely eczema”; NRSV “only an eruption”; NLT “only a temporary rash.”
Heb “and he shall wash his clothes.”

verses.zh: 但他为得洁净，将身体给祭司察看以后，癣若在皮上发散开了，他要再将身体给祭司察看。
verses.en: If, however, the scab is spreading further[NOTE:1] on the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his purification, then he must show himself to the priest a second time.
notes: Heb “And if spreading [infinitive absolute] it spreads [finite verb].” For the infinitive absolute used to highlight contrast rather than emphasis see GKC 343 §113.p.

verses.zh: 祭司要察看，癣若在皮上发散，就要定他为不洁净，是大麻疯。
verses.en: The priest must then examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the scab has spread on the skin, then the priest is to pronounce the person unclean.[NOTE:3] It is a disease.
notes: The “it” is not expressed but is to be understood. It refers to the “infection” (cf. the note on v. 2 above).
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ, cf. the note on v. 3 above).

verses.zh: 「人有了大麻疯的灾病，就要将他带到祭司面前。
verses.en: “When someone has a diseased infection,[NOTE:1] he must be brought to the priest.
notes: Heb “When there is an infection of disease in a man.” The term for “a man; a human being” (אָדָם, ʾadam; see the note on Lev 1:2 and cf. v. 2 above) refers to any person among “mankind,” male or female. For the rendering “diseased infection” see the note on v. 2 above.

verses.zh: 祭司要察看，皮上若长了白疖，使毛变白，在长白疖之处有了红瘀肉，
verses.en: The priest will then examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] a white swelling is on the skin, it has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see.” The pronoun “it” is unexpressed, but it should be assumed and it refers to the infection (cf. the note on v. 8 above).
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “and rawness [i.e., something living] of living flesh is in the swelling”; KJV, NASB, NRSV “quick raw flesh.”

verses.zh: 这是肉皮上的旧大麻疯，祭司要定他为不洁净，不用将他关锁，因为他是不洁净了。
verses.en: it is a chronic[NOTE:1] disease on the skin of his body,[NOTE:2] so the priest is to pronounce him unclean.[NOTE:3] The priest[NOTE:4] must not merely quarantine him, for he is unclean.[NOTE:5]
notes: The term rendered here “chronic” is a Niphal participle meaning “grown old” (HALOT 448 s.v. II ישׁן nif.2). The idea is that this is an old enduring skin disease that keeps on developing or recurring.
Heb “in the skin of his flesh” as opposed to the head or the beard (v. 29; cf. v. 2 above).
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ, cf. the note on v. 3 above).
Heb “he”; the referent (the priest) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Instead of just the normal quarantine isolation, this condition calls for the more drastic and enduring response stated in Lev 13:45-46. Raw flesh, of course, sometimes oozes blood to one degree or another, and blood flows are by nature impure (see, e.g., Lev 12 and 15; cf. J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 191).

verses.zh: 大麻疯若在皮上四外发散，长满了患灾病人的皮，据祭司察看，从头到脚无处不有，
verses.en: If, however, the disease breaks out[NOTE:1] on the skin so that the disease covers all the skin of the person with the infection[NOTE:2] from his head to his feet, as far as the priest can see,[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “And if spreading [infinitive absolute] it spreads out [finite verb].” For the infinitive absolute used to highlight contrast rather than emphasis see GKC 343 §113.p.
Heb “all the skin of the infection,” but see v. 4 above.
Heb “to all the appearance of the eyes of the priest.”

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看，全身的肉若长满了大麻疯，就要定那患灾病的为洁净；全身都变为白，他乃洁净了。
verses.en: the priest must then examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the disease covers his whole body, he is to pronounce the person with the infection clean.[NOTE:3] He has turned all white, so he is clean.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see.” The pronoun “it” is unexpressed, but it should be assumed and it refers to the infection (cf. the note on v. 8 above).
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV, NASB).
Heb “he shall pronounce the infection clean,” but see v. 4 above. Also, this is another use of the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher; cf. the note on v. 6 above).
Heb “all of him has turned white, and he is clean.”

verses.zh: 但红肉几时显在他的身上就几时不洁净。
verses.en: But whenever raw flesh appears in it,[NOTE:1] he will be unclean,
notes: Heb “and in the day of there appears in it living flesh.” Some English versions render this as “open sores” (cf. NCV, TEV, NLT).

verses.zh: 祭司一看那红肉就定他为不洁净。红肉本是不洁净，是大麻疯。
verses.en: so the priest is to examine the raw flesh[NOTE:1] and pronounce him unclean[NOTE:2]—it is diseased.
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see the living flesh.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ; cf. the note on v. 3 above).

verses.zh: 红肉若复原，又变白了，他就要来见祭司。
verses.en: If, however,[NOTE:1] the raw flesh once again turns white,[NOTE:2] then he must come to the priest.
notes: Heb “Or if/when.”

Heb “the living flesh returns and is turned/changed to white.” The Hebrew verb “returns” is שׁוּב (shuv), which often functions adverbially when combined with a second verb as it is here (cf. “and is turned”) and, in such cases, is usually rendered “again” (see, e.g., GKC 386-87 §120.g). Another suggestion is that here שׁוּב means “to recede” (cf., e.g., 2 Kgs 20:9), so one could translate “the raw flesh recedes and turns white.” This would mean that the new “white” skin “has grown over” the raw flesh (B. A. Levine, Leviticus [JPSTC], 79).

verses.zh: 祭司要察看，灾病处若变白了，祭司就要定那患灾病的为洁净，他乃洁净了。
verses.en: The priest will then examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the infection has turned white, the priest is to pronounce the person with the infection clean[NOTE:3]—he is clean.
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see it.”
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV, NASB).
Heb “the priest shall pronounce the infection clean,” but see v. 4 above. Also, this is another use of the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher, cf. the note on v. 6 above).

verses.zh: 「人若在皮肉上长疮，却治好了，
verses.en: “When someone’s body has a boil on its skin[NOTE:1] and it heals,
notes: Heb (MT) reads, “And flesh if/when there is in it, in its skin, a boil.” Smr has only “in it,” not “in its skin,” and a few medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate have only “in its skin” (cf. v. 24 below), not “in it.” It does not effect the meaning of the verse, but one is tempted to suggest that “in it” (בוֹ, vo) was added in error as a partial dittography from the beginning of “in its skin” (בְעֹרוֹ, veʿoro).

verses.zh: 在长疮之处又起了白疖，或是白中带红的火斑，就要给祭司察看。
verses.en: and in the place of the boil there is a white swelling or a reddish white bright spot, he must show himself to the priest.[NOTE:1]
notes: Some English versions translate “it shall be shown to [or “be seen by”] the priest,” taking the infection to be the subject of the verb (e.g., KJV, NASB, RSV, NRSV). Based on the Hebrew grammar there is no way to be sure which is intended.

verses.zh: 祭司要察看，若现象洼于皮，其上的毛也变白了，就要定他为不洁净，是大麻疯的灾病发在疮中。
verses.en: The priest will then examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] it appears to be deeper than the skin[NOTE:3] and its hair has turned white, then the priest is to pronounce the person unclean.[NOTE:4] It is a diseased infection that has broken out in the boil.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see.” The pronoun “it” is unexpressed, but it should be assumed and it refers to the infection (cf. the note on v. 8 above).
Heb “and behold.”

Heb “and behold its appearance is low (שָׁפָל, shafal) ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, “lower than”) the skin.” Compare “deeper” in v. 3 above where, however, a different word is used (עָמֹק, ʿamoq), and see the note on “swelling” in v. 1 above (cf. J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 192; note that, contrary to the MT, one Hebrew ms (Cairo Geniza) has עָמֹק in this verse as well as v. 4). The alternation of these two terms (i.e., “deeper” and “lower”) in vv. 25-26 below shows that they both refer to the same phenomenon. Some have argued that “this sore was lower than the surrounding skin” (J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:773, 788), in which case “swelling” would be an inappropriate translation of שְׂאֵת (seʾet) in v. 19. It seems unlikely, however, that the surface of a “boil” would sink below the surface of the surrounding skin. The infectious pus etc. that makes up a boil normally causes swelling.
The declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ, cf. the note on v. 3 above).
Heb “It is an infection of disease. In the boil it has broken out.” For the rendering “diseased infection” see the note on v. 2 above.

verses.zh: 祭司若察看，其上没有白毛，也没有洼于皮，乃是发暗，就要将他关锁七天。
verses.en: If, however,[NOTE:1] the priest examines it, and[NOTE:2] there is no white hair in it, it is not deeper than the skin, and it has faded, then the priest is to quarantine him for seven days.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and if.”
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV, NASB).
Heb “and the priest will shut him up seven days.”

verses.zh: 若在皮上发散开了，祭司就要定他为不洁净，是灾病。
verses.en: If[NOTE:1] it is spreading farther[NOTE:2] on the skin, then the priest is to pronounce him unclean.[NOTE:3] It is an infection.
notes: Heb “and if.”
Heb “is indeed spreading.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ, cf. the note on v. 3 above).

verses.zh: 火斑若在原处止住，没有发散，便是疮的痕迹，祭司就要定他为洁净。
verses.en: But if the bright spot stays in its place and has not spread,[NOTE:1] it is the scar of the boil, so the priest is to pronounce him clean.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and if under it the bright spot stands, it has not spread.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher, cf. the note on v. 6 above).

verses.zh: 「人的皮肉上若起了火毒，火毒的瘀肉成了火斑，或是白中带红的，或是全白的，
verses.en: “When a body has a burn on its skin[NOTE:1] and the raw area of the burn becomes a reddish white or white bright spot,
notes: Heb “Or a body, if there is in its skin a burn of fire.”

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看，火斑中的毛若变白了，现象又深于皮，是大麻疯在火毒中发出，就要定他为不洁净，是大麻疯的灾病。
verses.en: the priest must examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the hair has turned white in the bright spot and it appears to be deeper than the skin,[NOTE:3] it is a disease that has broken out in the burn.[NOTE:4] The priest is to pronounce the person unclean.[NOTE:5] It is a diseased infection.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see it.”
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “and its appearance is deep ‘from’ [comparative מִן (min) meaning ‘deeper than’] the skin.”
Heb “it is a disease. In the burn it has broken out.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ; cf. the note on v. 3 above).
For the rendering “diseased infection” see the note on v. 2 above.

verses.zh: 但是祭司察看，在火斑中若没有白毛，也没有洼于皮，乃是发暗，就要将他关锁七天。
verses.en: If, however,[NOTE:1] the priest examines it and[NOTE:2] there is no white hair in the bright spot, it is not deeper than the skin,[NOTE:3] and it has faded, then the priest is to quarantine him for seven days.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and if.”
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV); NASB “and indeed.”
Heb “and low it is not ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, “lower than”) the skin.” See the note on v. 20 above. Cf. TEV “not deeper than the surrounding skin.”
Heb “and the priest will shut him up seven days.”

verses.zh: 到第七天，祭司要察看他，火斑若在皮上发散开了，就要定他为不洁净，是大麻疯的灾病。
verses.en: The priest must then examine it on the seventh day, and if it is spreading further[NOTE:1] on the skin, then the priest is to pronounce him unclean. It is a diseased infection.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “is indeed spreading.”
For the rendering “diseased infection” see the note on v. 2 above.

verses.zh: 火斑若在原处止住，没有在皮上发散，乃是发暗，是起的火毒，祭司要定他为洁净，不过是火毒的痕迹。
verses.en: But if the bright spot stays in its place, has not spread on the skin,[NOTE:1] and it has faded, then it is the swelling of the burn, so the priest is to pronounce him clean,[NOTE:2] because it is the scar of the burn.
notes: Heb “and if under it the bright spot stands, it has not spread in the skin.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher; cf. the note on v. 6 above).

verses.zh: 「无论男女，若在头上有灾病，或是男人胡须上有灾病，
verses.en: “When a man or a woman has an infection on the head or in the beard,[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “And a man or a woman if there is in him an infection in head or in beard.” sn The shift here is from diseases that are on the (relatively) bare skin of the body to the scalp area of the male or female head or the bearded area of the male face.

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看；这灾病现象若深于皮，其间有细黄毛，就要定他为不洁净，这是头疥，是头上或是胡须上的大麻疯。
verses.en: the priest is to examine the infection,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] it appears to be deeper than the skin[NOTE:3] and the hair in it is reddish yellow and thin, then the priest is to pronounce the person unclean.[NOTE:4] It is scall,[NOTE:5] a disease of the head or the beard.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see the infection.”
Heb “and behold.”
Heb “its appearance is deep ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, “deeper than”) the skin.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָמֵא (tameʾ; cf. the note on v. 3 above).

The exact identification of this disease is unknown. Cf. KJV “dry scall”; NASB “a scale”; NIV84, NCV, NRSV “an itch”; NLT “a contagious skin disease.” For a discussion of “scall” disease in the hair, which is a crusty scabby disease of the skin under the hair that also affects the hair itself, see J. E. Hartley, Leviticus (WBC), 192-93, and J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:793-94. The Hebrew word rendered “scall” (נֶתֶק, neteq) is related to a verb meaning “to tear; to tear out; to tear apart.” It may derive from the scratching and/or the tearing out of the hair or the scales of the skin in response to the itching sensation caused by the disease.
Heb “It is scall. It is the disease of the head or the beard.”

verses.zh: 祭司若察看头疥的灾病，现象不深于皮，其间也没有黑毛，就要将长头疥灾病的关锁七天。
verses.en: But if the priest examines the scall infection and it does not appear to be deeper than the skin,[NOTE:1] and there is no black hair in it, then the priest is to quarantine the person with the scall infection for seven days.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and behold there is not its appearance deep ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, meaning “deeper than”) the skin.”
Heb “and the priest will shut up the infection of the scall seven days.”

verses.zh: 第七天，祭司要察看灾病，若头疥没有发散，其间也没有黄毛，头疥的现象不深于皮，
verses.en: The priest must then examine the infection on the seventh day, and if[NOTE:1] the scall has not spread, there is no reddish yellow hair in it, and the scall does not appear to be deeper than the skin,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “and the appearance of the scall is not deep ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, meaning “deeper than”) the skin.”

verses.zh: 那人就要剃去须发，但他不可剃头疥之处。祭司要将那长头疥的，再关锁七天。
verses.en: then the individual is to shave himself,[NOTE:1] but he must not shave the area affected by the scall,[NOTE:2] and the priest is to quarantine the person with the scall for another seven days.[NOTE:3]
notes: The shaving is done by the one who has the infection. Although KJV, ASV have the passive “he shall be shaven” here, most modern English versions have the reflexive “shall shave himself” (so NAB).
Heb “but the scall shall he not shave” (so KJV, ASV); NIV11 “except for the affected area.”
Heb “and the priest will shut up the scall a second seven days.”

verses.zh: 第七天，祭司要察看头疥，头疥若没有在皮上发散，现象也不深于皮，就要定他为洁净，他要洗衣服，便成为洁净。
verses.en: The priest must then examine the scall on the seventh day, and if[NOTE:1] the scall has not spread on the skin and it does not appear to be deeper than the skin,[NOTE:2] then the priest is to pronounce him clean.[NOTE:3] So he is to wash his clothes and be clean.
notes: Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “and its appearance is not deep ‘from’ (comparative מִן, min, meaning “deeper than”) the skin.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher, cf. the note on v. 6 above).

verses.zh: 但他得洁净以后，头疥若在皮上发散开了，
verses.en: If, however, the scall spreads further[NOTE:1] on the skin after his purification,
notes: Heb “And if spreading (infinitive absolute) it spreads further (finite verb).” For the infinitive absolute used to highlight contrast rather than emphasis see GKC 343 §113.p.

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看他。头疥若在皮上发散，就不必找那黄毛，他是不洁净了。
verses.en: then the priest is to examine it, and if[NOTE:1] the scall has spread on the skin, the priest is not to search further for reddish yellow hair.[NOTE:2] The person[NOTE:3] is unclean.
notes: Heb “and behold.”
Heb “the priest shall not search to the reddish yellow hair.”
Heb “he”; the referent (the affected person) is specified in the translation for clarity (likewise in the following verse).

verses.zh: 祭司若看头疥已经止住，其间也长了黑毛，头疥已然痊愈，那人是洁净了，就要定他为洁净。
verses.en: If, as far as the priest can see, the scall has stayed the same[NOTE:1] and black hair has sprouted in it, the scall has been healed; the person is clean. So the priest is to pronounce him clean.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and if in his eyes the infection has stood.”
This is the declarative Piel of the verb טָהֵר (taher, cf. the note on v. 6 above).

verses.zh: 「无论男女，皮肉上若起了火斑，就是白火斑，
verses.en: “When a man or a woman has bright spots—white bright spots—on the skin of their body,

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看，他们肉皮上的火斑若白中带黑，这是皮上发出的白癣，那人是洁净了。
verses.en: the priest is to examine them,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the bright spots on the skin of their body are faded white, it is a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin. The person is clean.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see.”
Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).
Heb “he,” but the regulation applies to a man or a woman (v. 38a). In the translation “the person” is used to specify the referent more clearly.

verses.zh: 「人头上的发若掉了，他不过是头秃，还是洁净。
verses.en: “When a man’s head is bare so that he is balding in back,[NOTE:1] he is clean.
notes: Heb “And a man, when his head is rubbed bare, he is bald-headed.” The translation offered here, referring to the back of the head (i.e., the area from the top of the head sloping backwards), is based on the contrast between this condition and that of the following verse. See also B. A. Levine, Leviticus (JPSTC), 82.

verses.zh: 他顶前若掉了头发，他不过是顶门秃，还是洁净。
verses.en: If his head is bare on the forehead[NOTE:1] so that he is balding in front,[NOTE:2] he is clean.
notes: Heb “And if from the front edge of his face, his head is rubbed bare.” See the note on v. 40 above.
The rendering “balding in front” corresponds to the location of the bareness at the beginning of the verse.

verses.zh: 头秃处或是顶门秃处若有白中带红的灾病，这就是大麻疯发在他头秃处或是顶门秃处，
verses.en: But if there is a reddish white infection in the back or front bald area, it is a disease breaking out in his back or front bald area.

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看，他起的那灾病若在头秃处或是顶门秃处有白中带红的，像肉皮上大麻疯的现象，
verses.en: The priest is to examine it,[NOTE:1] and if[NOTE:2] the swelling of the infection is reddish white in the back or the front bald area like the appearance of a disease on the skin of the body,[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and the priest shall see it” (cf. KJV). The MT has “him/it” which some take to refer to the person as a whole (i.e., “him”; see, e.g., J. Milgrom, Leviticus [AB], 1:770; NIV, NRSV, etc.), while others take it as a reference to the “infection” (נֶגַע, negaʿ) in v. 42 (J. E. Hartley, Leviticus [WBC], 172, 177). Smr has “her/it,” which would probably refer to “disease” (צָרַעַת, tsaraʿat) in v. 42. The general pattern in the chapter suggests that “it,” either the infection or the disease, is the object of the examination (see, e.g., v. 3 above and v. 50 below).
Heb “and behold.”
Heb “like appearance of disease of skin of flesh.”

verses.zh: 那人就是长大麻疯，不洁净的，祭司总要定他为不洁净，他的灾病是在头上。
verses.en: he is a diseased man. He is unclean. The priest must surely pronounce him unclean because of his infection on his head.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or perhaps translate, “His infection [is] on his head,” as a separate independent sentence (cf. KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV). There is no causal expression in the Hebrew text connecting these two clauses, but the logical relationship between them seems to be causal.

verses.zh: 「身上有长大麻疯灾病的，他的衣服要撕裂，也要蓬头散发，蒙着上唇，喊叫说：『不洁净了！不洁净了！』
verses.en: “As for the diseased person who has the infection,[NOTE:1] his clothes must be torn, the hair of his head must be unbound, he must cover his mustache,[NOTE:2] and he must call out ‘Unclean! Unclean!’
notes: Heb “And the diseased one who in him is the infection.”

Heb “and his head shall be unbound, and he shall cover on [his] mustache.” Tearing one’s clothing, allowing the hair to hang loose rather than bound up in a turban, and covering the mustache on the upper lip are all ways of expressing shame, grief, or distress (cf., e.g., Lev 10:6 and Micah 3:7).

verses.zh: 灾病在他身上的日子，他便是不洁净；他既是不洁净，就要独居营外。」
verses.en: The whole time he has the infection[NOTE:1] he will be continually unclean. He must live in isolation, and his place of residence must be outside the camp.
notes: Heb “All the days which the infection is in him.”

verses.zh: 「染了大麻疯灾病的衣服，无论是羊毛衣服、是麻布衣服，
verses.en: “When a garment has a diseased infection in it,[NOTE:1] whether a wool or linen garment,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And the garment, if there is in it a mark of disease.”
Heb “in a wool garment or in a linen garment.”

verses.zh: 无论是在经上、在纬上，是麻布的、是羊毛的，是在皮子上，或在皮子做的甚么物件上，
verses.en: or in the warp or woof[NOTE:1] of the linen or the wool, or in leather or anything made of leather,[NOTE:2]
notes: The warp (vertical) and woof (horizontal) thread may be two different sets of thread not yet woven together, or they may refer to two different kinds of thread already woven, in which case one might have the disease in it while the other does not. See the explanation in J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:809-10.
Heb “in any handiwork of skin” (cf. KJV, ASV, NRSV); most other modern English versions have “leather.”

verses.zh: 或在衣服上、皮子上，经上、纬上，或在皮子做的甚么物件上，这灾病若是发绿，或是发红，是大麻疯的灾病，要给祭司察看。
verses.en: if the infection[NOTE:1] in the garment or leather or warp or woof or any article of leather is yellowish green or reddish, it is a diseased infection, and it must be shown to the priest.
notes: Heb “and the infection is.” This clause is conditional in force, and is translated as such by almost all English versions.

verses.zh: 祭司就要察看那灾病，把染了灾病的物件关锁七天。
verses.en: The priest is to examine and then quarantine the article with the infection for seven days.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “And the priest shall see the infection and he shall shut up the infection seven days.”

verses.zh: 第七天，他要察看那灾病，灾病或在衣服上，经上、纬上，皮子上，若发散，这皮子无论当作何用，这灾病是蚕食的大麻疯，都是不洁净了。
verses.en: He must then examine the infection on the seventh day. If the infection has spread in the garment, or in the warp, or in the woof, or in the leather—whatever the article into which the leather was made[NOTE:1]—the infection is a malignant disease. It is unclean.
notes: Heb “to all which the leather was made into a handiwork.”

verses.zh: 那染了灾病的衣服，或是经上、纬上，羊毛上，麻衣上，或是皮子做的甚么物件上，他都要焚烧；因为这是蚕食的大麻疯，必在火中焚烧。
verses.en: He must burn the garment or the warp or the woof, whether wool or linen, or any article of leather which has the infection in it. Because it is a malignant disease it must be burned up in the fire.

verses.zh: 「祭司要察看，若灾病在衣服上，经上、纬上，或是皮子做的甚么物件上，没有发散，
verses.en: But if the priest examines it and[NOTE:1] the infection has not spread in the garment or in the warp or in the woof or in any article of leather,
notes: Heb “And if the priest sees and behold”; NASB “and indeed.”

verses.zh: 祭司就要吩咐他们，把染了灾病的物件洗了，再关锁七天。
verses.en: the priest is to command that they wash whatever has the infection and quarantine it for another seven days.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “a second seven days.”

verses.zh: 洗过以后，祭司要察看，那物件若没有变色，灾病也没有消散，那物件就不洁净，是透重的灾病，无论正面反面，都要在火中焚烧。
verses.en: The priest must then examine it after the infection has been washed out, and if[NOTE:1] the infection has not changed its appearance[NOTE:2] even though the infection has not spread, it is unclean. You must burn it up in the fire. It is a fungus, whether on the back side or front side of the article.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and behold” (so KJV, ASV).

Heb “the infection has not changed its eye.” Smr has “its/his eyes,” as in vv. 5 and 37, but here it refers to the appearance of the article of cloth or leather, unlike vv. 5 and 37 where there is a preposition attached and it refers to the eyes of the priest.

The terms “back side” and “front side” are the same as those used in v. 42 for the “back or front bald area” of a man’s head. The exact meaning of these terms when applied to articles of cloth or leather is uncertain. It could refer, for example, to the inside versus the outside of a garment, or the back versus the front side of an article of cloth or leather. See J. Milgrom, Leviticus (AB), 1:814, for various possibilities.

verses.zh: 洗过以后，祭司要察看，若见那灾病发暗，他就要把那灾病从衣服上、皮子上、经上、纬上，都撕去。
verses.en: But if the priest has examined it and[NOTE:1] the infection has faded after it has been washed, he is to tear it out of[NOTE:2] the garment or the leather or the warp or the woof.
notes: Heb “And if the priest saw and behold….”
Heb “and he shall tear it from.”

verses.zh: 若仍现在衣服上，或是经上、纬上、皮子做的甚么物件上，这就是灾病又发了、必用火焚烧那染灾病的物件。
verses.en: Then if[NOTE:1] it still appears again in the garment or the warp or the woof, or in any article of leather, it is an outbreak. Whatever has the infection in it you must burn up in the fire.
notes: Heb “And if”; NIV, NCV “But if”; NAB “If, however.”

verses.zh: 所洗的衣服，或是经，或是纬，或是皮子做的甚么物件，若灾病离开了，要再洗，就洁净了。」
verses.en: But the garment or the warp or the woof or any article of leather which you wash and infection disappears from it[NOTE:1] is to be washed a second time, and it will be clean.”
notes: Heb “and the infection turns aside from them.”

verses.zh: 这就是大麻疯灾病的条例，无论是在羊毛衣服上，麻布衣服上，经上、纬上，和皮子做的甚么物件上，可以定为洁净或是不洁净。
verses.en: This is the law[NOTE:1] of the diseased infection in the garment of wool or linen, or the warp or woof, or any article of leather, for pronouncing it clean or unclean.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew term translated “law” (תּוֹרָה, torah) introduces here a summary or colophon for all of Lev 13. Similar summaries are found in Lev 7:37-38; 11:46-47; 14:54-57; and 15:32-33.
These are declarative Piel forms of the verbs טָהֵר (taher) and טָמֵא (tameʾ) respectively (cf. the notes on vv. 3 and 6 above).

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT THE PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation
of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must
not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects. Compare your subject divisions with the five translations
above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation.
Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

- First paragraph

- Second paragraph

- Etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Leviticus 13-14 forms a unified context based on uncleanness in humans, garments, houses.

- Brief Outline of Leviticus 13-14

- Lev. 13:1-46, unclean skin diseases in humans

- swelling (BDB 673)

- scab (BDB 705, JPSOA, "rash")

- bright spot (BDB 97, JPSOA, "discoloration")

- other skin problems

- Lev. 13:47-55, unclean marks in fabrics

- Lev. 14:1-32, procedures for cleansing

- Lev. 14:33-53, deals with marks in houses and how to make them clean

- Lev. 14:54-57, typical editorial summary of the laws of "leprosy"

- There are several types of skin diseases discussed here.

- a swelling

- a scab

- a bright spot

- the collective term "leprosy"
However, most modern physicians assume that this does not include what we know today as
leprosy. The reason for this is that the priest had the option of quarantining the person for seven
or fourteen days and then making a determination according to the progression of the disease.
Modern leprosy is a very slow developing disease and would, therefore, be excluded from this
criteria. This context would involve things such as eczema or skin diseases which have an oozing
fluid or which are highly contagious and would affect the entire community. This does show that
the rights of the individual were limited to the rights and well-being of the community.

- For a good discussion of "leprosy" in Leviticus, see ABD, vol. 4, pp. 277-282.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 13:1-8

1Then the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, 2"When a
man has on the skin of his body a swelling or a scab or a bright spot, and it becomes an infection of leprosy on the skin of
his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests. 3The priest shall look
at the mark on the skin of the body, and if the hair in the infection has turned white and the infection appears to be deeper
than the skin of his body, it is an infection of leprosy; when the priest has looked at him, he shall pronounce him unclean.
4But if the bright spot is white on the skin of his body, and it does not appear to be deeper than the skin, and
the hair on it has not turned white, then the priest shall isolate him who has the infection for seven days.
5The priest shall look at him on the seventh day, and if in his eyes the infection has not changed and
the infection has not spread on the skin, then the priest shall isolate him for seven more days. 6The priest shall
look at him again on the seventh day, and if the infection has faded and the mark has not spread on the skin, then the priest
shall pronounce him clean; it is only a scab. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean. 7"But if the scab
spreads farther on the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall appear again to the priest.
8The priest shall look, and if the scab has spread on the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is leprosy."

13:1 This opening phrase matches Lev. 11:1, but not Lev. 12:1. One wonders why. The book of Leviticus
is an editorial process over a long period of time. Much goes back to the Tabernacle, but not all.

▣ "man" This is the term adam (BDB 9, Lev. 13:9) used in a generic sense
(i.e., any person, cf. Lev. 13:29,38).

13:2 "swelling" The MT has "swelling" (BDB 673, NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 737, #2), but AB, p. 773, suggests that it
does not come from the VERBAL root "to lift" or "to rise," but advocates the translation of the Targums.

- deep spot (i.e., indented)

- prominent mark

- mark

▣ "scab" See note at Lev. 13:6.

▣ "a bright spot" This translates "spot" (BDB 97); it may relate to

- an eruption of bodily fluids

- a feverish, discolored place (whitish and hot, like a boil), cf Lev. 13:10,19

▣

NASB
"an infection of leprosy"

NKJV
"a leprous sore"

NRSV, LXX
"a leprous disease"

TEV
"dreaded skin disease"

NJB
"a contagious skin disease"

JPSOA
"scaly affection"

The MT has "mark" or "stroke" (BDB 619, #3) CONSTRUCT "leprosy" (BDB 863) but
see note in Contextual Insights, C.

13:3 The priest is to be the one to test the different kinds of skin diseases. A brief outline of the type of tests
would help us see the structure of this chapter.

- Lev. 13:10-17 deals with raw flesh

- Lev. 13:18-23 deals with boils (NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 81)

- Lev. 13:24-28 deals with burns

- Lev. 13:29-37 deals with head infections

- Lev. 13:38-39 deals with eczema (white spots)

- Lev. 13:40-44 deals with baldness

▣ "look" This VERB (BDB 906, KB 1157) is used often in the sense of "examine
(cf. Lev. 13:3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15, 17, 20, 21, 25, 26, 27, 30, 31, 32, 34, 36, 39, 43, 50, 51, 53, 55, 56, 57). The priests
were responsible for the spiritual and physical health of the community. Israel must be a people without blemish because
they represented "the holy one of Israel" (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE).

▣ "hair" In the context of Leviticus 13-14 human hair color in an infected area is mentioned several times
as a way to determine "clean" or "unclean."

- white ‒ Lev. 13:3-4,10,21,25,26

- yellow ‒ Lev. 13:30,32,36

- black ‒ Lev. 13:31,37

Being "unclean" excluded one from worship and also, in certain cases, from community.

13:4 "isolate" This VERB (BDB 688, KB 742, Hiphil PERFECT
with waw) is used for quarantining a contagious person from the community (cf. Lev. 13:4, 5, 11, 21, 26, 31, 33, 50 ,54;
14:38,46). Miriam is isolated for leprosy in Num. 12:14-15. Usually it was for a specific period of time.

- seven days

- fourteen days

- permanently until healing or death

There is another possible meaning that "isolate" relates to the sore, possibly drawing a line around it
to see if it spreads.

13:5 "seventh day" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4.

▣ "spread" This VERB (BDB 832, KB 979) occurs only in this literary unit (i.e., Leviticus 13-14),
but it occurs 22 times. Spreading was one of the criteria for determining if someone/something was "unclean."

13:6 Notice the criteria the priest used to pronounce an infected person clean.

- the infection (BDB 619, lit. "mark" or "stroke") has faded

- it has not spread

▣

NASB, NJB, Peshitta
"a scab"

NKJV, TEV
"a sore"

NRSV
"an eruption"

JPSOA
"a rash"

LXX
"a mark"

This term (תחפס, BDB 705, KB 764) occurs only here (Lev. 13:2, 6, 7, 8)

and Lev. 14:56. Its meaning is uncertain. KB lists a related root from Ethiopia (KB 764 III), which means "spread out" or from KB 764 II,
"make scabby" (i.e., related to חפס).

It may relate to חפס (BDB I, II) to "pour," i.e., eruption of fluids.

13:7 "spreads farther" This grammatical construct of intensity (i.e., an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
and an IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, BDB 832, KB 979) appears four times (i.e., Lev. 13:7, 22, 27, 35).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 13:9-17

13:9-10 There is a distinction between "the mark" or "the stroke" (BDB 619) of Lev. 13:2 and 13:9. But

In Lev. 13:10 there are new criteria for judging.

- hair in the spot is also white

- raw flesh (cf. Lev. 13:14-15)

This type of skin disease must be isolated.

13:10 "swelling" The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 737, suggests several different translations for this Hebrew word.

- white blotch ‒ Lev. 13:10,19

- scar/blotch of a burn ‒ Lev. 13:28

- inflamed swelling ‒ Lev. 13:43

There are so many of these terms describing medical conditions that moderns are not sure about.
Obviously, they were terms of their ANE vocabulary which do not fit or conform to modern medical terminology.

13:45-46 "As for the leper who had the infection" This is a series of procedures which a person designated
as "unclean" must perform in order to warn his covenant partners of his ceremonial contamination.

- He shall tear his clothes in a symbolic fashion of mourning.

- He shall let the hair of his head go unkempt.

- he shall cover his mustache.

- He shall cry, "Unclean! Unclean!"

- From 2 Kgs. 7:3, we also know that lepers may have lived in colonies outside the camp.

Leprosy was a terrible disease because it excluded one from the normal joys of life and from his or her
own family. Some would see by this that leprosy was a divine punishment for sin, somewhat like barrenness in women.
However, they base this on Uzziah's getting leprosy because he disobeyed God, but making a general statement is
probably inappropriate.
